title: Roman calumny: Protestants make absolute certainty of pardon the essence of justifying faith
source_text: I. Inter varias calumnias quibus Protestantium Doctrina in Justificationis negotio impetitur, hae quoque frequenter occurrunt, Quod communi consensu doceant, Omnes & singulos homines posse & debere certa fide credere sibi fuisse remissa peccata, & se coram Deo justos esse. Id illis tam firmiter persuasum esse debere, quam hoc Jesum Christum esse Dei Filium & mundi Redemptorem, & similia fidei dogmata. Talem persuasionem ita necessariam esse, ut absque ea nemo vere fidelis & justus esse possit; non secus ac si credere detractaret aliquem ex praecipuis & fundamentalibus fidei articulis. In ejusmodi persuasione fidem veram & salvificam constituendam esse, tanquam in ejus actu proprio atque praecipuo. Adeoque homines tali fide, & quidem sola, coram Deo justificari, licet alioqui vitiis indulgeant, nec studeant bonis operibus.
pass_a_gloss: Among the calumnies with which Protestant doctrine on justification is attacked, these also frequently occur: that by common consent they teach every single person can and ought by a certain faith to believe his sins have been remitted and that he is just before God; that this must be as firmly persuaded to them as that Jesus Christ is the Son of God and Redeemer of the world, and like articles of faith; that such persuasion is so necessary that without it no one can be truly faithful and just, no less than if he refused to believe one of the chief fundamental articles; that true saving faith is to be placed in that persuasion as in its proper and principal act; and that therefore people are justified before God by such faith alone, even if they indulge vices and do not pursue good works.
pass_b_english: Romans often charge that Protestants make a firm persuasion of personal pardon the essence of saving faith.
They claim this certainty must match assent to Christ’s deity, that without it no one is truly faithful, and that it alone justifies even the vicious.
